title: Playing for the public: melody, the whistling test and keeping his own style
summary: Cobb argues for playing for laymen with melodies they can whistle, criticizes too many notes in modern jazz, and insists on staying Arnett Cobb.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: And if they can relate to whatever you are doing today, simplicity, they buy that. But I'm not playing for musicians. I play for the general public, and the general public and the laymen don't talk about no whole lot of chord changes, how many notes you play. They go by what they feel.

Here's a guy says to you, I don't know what you're doing, but I don't -- I don't feel it. I know it ain't right. To him it's not right, because he doesn't feel it, and that's what you got to depend on at the box office. (Inaudible) right with him.

I'll give you another thing. I'd just lay in my bed before day in the morning, and my house had a sidewalk. And you remember that thing, Tea for Two (inaudible)? The public can relate to this. They will whistle it up and down the sidewalk. Something they can hum. It was simple. I learned a lot from that. I'm lying in my bed, and people come and say, (whistling), before day in the morning, like 3:00 and 4:00 o'clock. I say, isn't this beautiful?
And I hear it on the jukebox and can't wait until
they're coming down to hear them playing it in person. That was my side of it.

Well, you know, if you take the big numbers of that period -- I mean if you take a thing like Stopping at the Savoy, Christopher Columbu, all these things had a -- they at least had a sort of riff that you'd whistle or hum.
Now, today you can't -- there's nothing that the average person can remember or whistle (inaudible).
Now you can see where I'm coming from.
Because there's too many notes involved. So may I ask you a question?
What are they trying to prove?

Yeah, but also, you know, I mean it's fine to whistle through those changes like they do, but they should be creating some sort of melody on that, you know, but it's too -- it's too much of an exercise. You (in-audible) well, I mean (inaudible) he's not swinging. There's no -- he's just running long outs to (inaudible). I thought it was terrible.
They have that thing that they're trying

to portray to the public, which is all right, what they do. I enjoy what they do, but I'm not going to do it. And I'm not going to change my style of playing because they've got some new music coming up, and I've got to fit that note. I've been in it too long. I'm going to be Arnett Cobb, and I was 20, 30, 40 years ago.
Well, that's how it should be.
(Inaudible). I've got to be me. I've got to be me -- you going to cut me off?

Well, also, I mean, you know, you developed something which is you and where, you know, when you are in your twenties, that's when you establish your musical personality. You can't be changing your personality to fit that of later generations.
